slides.text:
A flag is a named option the user passes to a command, like `--name Ana` or `--team=red`. The command declares which flags it accepts, and cobra reads them from the arguments when it runs.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
declare flag: name, default, usage
user runs: greet --name Ana
cobra parses the arguments
Run reads the value: "Ana"

slides.text: Every flag has a **name**, a **default** that is used when the user leaves it out, and a **usage** text. They are declared on the flag set of the command, `cmd.Flags()`, before `Execute` runs.

Three sessions:

- **Session 1:** string flags, and two ways to read them
- **Session 2:** bool and number flags, and shorthand letters
- **Session 3:** lists of values, flags on subcommands and telling a given flag from a default
A string flag is declared with a name, a default and a usage text. Do it before `Execute`, which is when cobra reads the arguments.

The user passes the value after the name, with a space or an equals sign:

- `app --lang es`
- `app --lang=es`

When the flag is left out, the default stays.

There are two ways to get the value:

- ask the flag set by name inside `Run`, with a getter
- bind the flag to a variable, and read the variable

Both give the same value.

slides.text: A bool flag needs no value: giving it turns it on, and it stays off when it is left out. `BoolVar` binds it to a bool variable, with `false` as the default.
slides.code:
var dryRun bool
cmd.Flags().BoolVar(
    &dryRun, "dry", false, "no changes",
)

slides.text: Numbers work the same way, with a number as the default: `Int` and `IntVar`, and also `Float64` and `Duration`, like `30s`. Cobra turns the text into the type, so the variable is already an `int`.
A `P` at the end of the method name adds a one-letter name after the long one. The user can then type `-w` instead of `--workers`.

exercises.title: Declare a bool flag
exercises.guide: Fill the method that gives the flag set and the one that declares a bool flag.

exercises.title: What does it print?
options: An error about the extra word
exercises.explanation: A bool flag never takes the next word as its value, so `--color` alone means `true` and `false` is left as a plain argument. Only `--color=false` turns it off.

exercises.title: Shorthand letters
exercises.guide: Give each flag a one-letter name.

chunks.guide: `quiet` hides the welcome line.
The `P` methods take a letter after the long name.

notes.text: The P adds a one-letter name after the long one.
Lets the user write -t instead of --team.

chunks.text:
rootCmd.Flags().StringVarP(
        &team, "team", "t", "blue", "your team",
    )
    rootCmd.Flags().BoolVarP(
        &quiet, "quiet", "q", false, "no hello",
    )
    rootCmd.Execute()

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.explanation: Shorthand letters of bool flags can be grouped: `-lq` is the same as `-l -q`, so both are on.

intro.title: Lists, scope and what was given

slides.text: A string slice flag collects many values into a `[]string`. The user can repeat the flag, or put commas between the values.
Each command has its own flag set, reached with its own `Flags()`. A flag declared on one command is not known by the others.
The value of a flag does not tell whether the user typed it: a typed value can equal the default. `Changed` asks the flag set, and is true only when the user gave the flag.

exercises.title: Many values
exercises.guide: One flag that can be given many times.

chunks.guide: `tags` is a slice that the flag fills.
A slice flag has no values unless the user gives them.

notes.text: Collects every value, repeated or with commas.
An empty slice when the flag is not given.

exercises.title: A flag on a subcommand
exercises.guide: Declare a flag on the subcommand that uses it.

chunks.guide: The `add` subcommand prints how many it added.
The root command only groups subcommands.
The flag goes on `addCmd`, the command that reads it.

notes.text: This flag belongs to add, not to the root.

chunks.text:
addCmd.Flags().IntVar(
        &copies, "copies", 1, "how many to add",
    )
    rootCmd.AddCommand(addCmd)
    rootCmd.Execute()

exercises.title: Who accepts the flag?
exercises.explanation: `Flags()` belongs to the command it is called on, here `addCmd`. The root and `listCmd` have their own flag sets.
